summary: Learners aged 9–11 learn how people protect endangered species by matching the right strategy to a specific threat — protected areas (national parks, marine reserves), captive breeding and reintroduction, anti-poaching patrols, wildlife corridors linking fragmented habitat, and laws banning trade (e.g. the CITES ivory ban). A central idea is that conservation must protect BOTH habitats AND individual species: breeding animals with nowhere safe to release them fails. Documented recoveries (California condor, Arabian oryx) show conservation can succeed, and learners identify concrete habitat-friendly actions children and families can take.
misconceptions: 'Just put endangered animals in zoos and they're saved' — captive breeding only works with habitat to release them back into; zoos alone aren't a solution.
'One strategy fixes every species' — different threats need different, matched interventions.
'Conservation never works / it's hopeless' — documented recoveries (condor, oryx) show it can succeed.
'Only scientists and governments can help' — individual and family choices affect habitats too.
'Protecting the animal is enough without protecting its habitat' — a species can't survive without the habitat it depends on.

activities.title: Save-the-species planning scenarios
steps: Take on the role of a conservation manager for a case species shown with its specific threats — for example poaching, a shrinking range, a population too small to recover on its own, or habitat cut into isolated patches.

Choose interventions from a fixed set — protected reserve, anti-poaching patrol, captive-breeding programme, wildlife corridor, trade ban — spending within a limited budget, so you must prioritise rather than pick everything.
Deliberately try saving a species with captive breeding alone first, then watch a recovery graph play the years forward and observe what happens to the population.
Add habitat protection to the captive-breeding case and re-run, comparing the two recovery curves.
Write down, for each case, which threat you were addressing and why your chosen strategy fits that threat.
activities.insight: Different threats need different, matched interventions, and species and habitat must be protected together: in this model, captive breeding alone plateaus because there is nowhere safe to release the young, and the wild population recovers once habitat is also protected. Real outcomes depend on the species and its threats.

activities.title: Match the threat to the strategy
steps: Sort a set of threats — poaching, habitat loss, a population too small to recover, habitat broken into isolated patches, international trade in animal parts — and pair each with the intervention that best addresses it (patrols for poaching; trade bans for illegal trade/demand; reserves for habitat loss; captive breeding for tiny populations; corridors for fragmentation).
Match named recovered species to the strategy that saved them (e.g. California condor and Arabian oryx to captive breeding and reintroduction).
Answer a short question on whether rising numbers of a bred animal in zoos means the species is saved, and justify the answer.
Explain in a sentence or two why protecting the habitat and helping the individual species have to happen together.
activities.insight: Learners can distinguish the strategies, link them to the threats they fit, and articulate that captive numbers alone do not equal a saved species.

activities.title: Talk with a conservation ranger
steps: Discuss in role with a conservation scientist or park ranger who describes a real recovery such as the California condor, including the hard choices and trade-offs behind it (funding limits, community needs, deciding what to prioritise).
Ask and answer questions about why a single success story still required years of effort and a protected place to return animals to.
Respond to the prompt: 'What is one thing you or your family could do that would genuinely help wildlife?' and explain how many small habitat-friendly actions add up.
activities.insight: Real conservation involves trade-offs, funding and community values voiced by people, and ordinary individuals and families can contribute through concrete habitat-friendly choices.

checkQuestion: A zoo successfully breeds lots of a rare tiger in its enclosures. A student says: 'Great — now the tiger is saved.' Is breeding them in the zoo enough to save the species? What else is needed?
checkAnswer: Breeding in captivity helps, but it isn't enough on its own. To truly save the species the tigers need a protected wild habitat to return to — forest with enough prey and space, kept safe from poaching and destruction. Without protected habitat the animals have nowhere to live wild, and the species survives only in cages. Real conservation protects habitats AND helps individual species (captive breeding, anti-poaching patrols, wildlife corridors, laws) together.
